newsitem.title: USA: Albright discusses Mideast with White House, cites hope.
newsitem.headline: Albright discusses Mideast with White House, cites hope.

text.p: Secretary of State Madeleine Albright met on Wednesday at the White House on the Middle East and said later she was hopeful of progress in reviving Israeli-Palestinian peace negotiations.
"I am hopeful this period that has been so difficult will come to an end," she said during an appearance before the Los Angeles World Affairs Council.

Albright, enroute to Asia, said she held talks on the Middle East at the White House before departing Washington for an overnight stop in Los Angeles. She gave no details on the who was at the meeting or what was discussed.

She said, however, that the United States continued to be "very concerned about the deteriorating situation in the Middle East" and to encourage Israelis and Palestinians to "take some of the hard decisions" needed to get the two parties back to the bargaining table.

"The Palestinians must understand the importance of security to the Israelis. The Isralies must understand the importance of not taking unilateral measures on permanent status (peace) issues," she said.
She said U.S. officials were "meeting hourly" on the matter and pledged that the Clinton administration is determined to stick with its mediating role in the region.

Earlier, State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns had called an Israeli-Palestinian meeting in Brussels on Tuesday positive and important but said it is still unclear if the two sides are moving closer to resuming peace talks.

The talks between Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat were "a good step forward" but he said it was "not possible to give you any kind of concrete examples that it's (the peace process) moving forward."
He spoke before being briefed by Albright on her White House meeting.
"We still have a long way to go before we can say that significant progress is being made," Burns told reporters accompanying Albright on her trip to Asia.
He said the European Union deserves credit for brokering the meeting.
After the Brussels talks, Levy and Arafat said they had made great strides in sweetening the bitterness of five months of acrimony over the deadlocked talks.
Neither would elaborate during a news conference on what they had agreed on to accelerate a possible return to the negotiating table but both stressed that the meeting was a breakthrough.
Israeli-Palestinian talks have been deadlocked since Israel started building a Jewish settlement in East Jerusalem in March, triggering Palestinian protests.
